For a buyer the practical points are the form bought, the basis a result is reported on, where the rapeseed Oil came from and the laboratory’s reporting limit. Testing finds contamination but does not remove it.

<a id="hmi-ing-002"></a>

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-rapeseed-oil" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-rapeseed-oil-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of rapeseed oil, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>WHO GEMS/Food is the only compatible sampling family for rapeseed oil, oil on this basis in the completed rapeseed oil ledger, so this single-family reference cannot represent other markets. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach rapeseed Oil

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach rapeseed Oil comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Rapeseed Oil, oil from pressed raw oil, fraction 1, one production lot had Fe higher at 3,250 µg/kg, against 630 µg/kg for extraction in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2016</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">A comparative study of the content of heavy metals in oils:</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

<a id="trade-offs-and-failure-modes"></a>
## Trade-offs and limits of controls

<a id="hmi-ing-022"></a>
<a id="can-an-intervention-increase-another-contaminant-or-redistribute-contamination-to-a-by-product"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-023"></a>
<a id="what-effects-on-nutrition-yield-sensory-quality-stability-and-waste-streams-were-measured"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-024"></a>
<a id="what-costs-constraints-adverse-effects-or-failure-modes-are-documented-and-which-are-unknown"></a>

Avoiding exposed growing areas lowered the metal measured in the studies available, but no study measured the cost or supply effect of doing so.<sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2016</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">A comparative study of the content of heavy metals in oils:</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Metals do not move together, so a lot that passes a lead limit says little about cadmium, arsenic or nickel unless those are tested as well.



<a id="sampling-and-testing"></a>
## Testing rapeseed Oil for metals

<a id="hmi-ing-025"></a>
<a id="what-sampling-design-is-appropriate-for-the-ingredient-heterogeneity-lot-and-decision"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-026"></a>
<a id="which-methods-species-measurements-validation-evidence-and-reporting-limits-are-needed"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-027"></a>
<a id="what-can-a-certificate-of-analysis-or-non-detect-establish-and-what-remains-untested"></a>

Results depend on the method and its reporting limit. Reporting limits for lead ranged from 2.5 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food) to 100 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a <a id="universal-faqs"></a>
## Rapeseed Oil FAQs

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-rapeseed-oil" data-anchor="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-rapeseed-oil" data-question="What heavy metals are found in rapeseed Oil?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What heavy metals are found in rapeseed Oil?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The library reports lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, total mercury, nickel, chromium, aluminium, tin, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, V, As and Ba in rapeseed Oil, most often lead, cadmium and total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/ashraf2012-heavy-metals-vegetable-oils-saudi-arabia|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ashraf MW · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ashraf2012-heavy-metals-vegetable-oils-saudi-arabia">Levels of Selected Heavy Metals in Varieties of Vegetable Oils Consumed in Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and Health Risk Assessment of Local Population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Asian Journal of Chemistry (Uncorrected Proof)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ashraf2012-heavy-metals-vegetable-oils-saudi-arabia">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/matei2025-vegetable-oils-romania-gfaas|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Matei N, Birghila S, Dobrinas S, Soceanu A, Popescu V, Zaharia (Pricopie) R-G · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/matei2025-vegetable-oils-romania-gfaas">Physicochemical Properties, Trace Elements, and Health Risk Assessment of Edible Vegetable Oils Consumed in Romania</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Applied Sciences</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/matei2025-vegetable-oils-romania-gfaas">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/lin2024-edible-oils-taiwan-12-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Lin S-T, Liao K-W, Xuan T-C, Chiou T-Y, Lin Z-E, Lee W-J · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-rapeseed-oil" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-rapeseed-oil" data-question="How do heavy metals get into rapeseed Oil?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into rapeseed Oil?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, rapeseed Oil from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than rapeseed Oil from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2016</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">A comparative study of the content of heavy metals in oils:</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Rapeseed Oil, oil from extraction had cadmium higher at 90 µg/kg, against 80 µg/kg for pressed bleached oil, fraction 4, one production lot in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2016</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">A comparative study of the content of heavy metals in oils:</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2016-a-comparative-study-of-the-content-of-heavy">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-rapeseed-oil-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-rapeseed-oil-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in rapeseed Oil is inorganic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much of the arsenic in rapeseed Oil is inorganic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Inorganic arsenic, the more toxic form, was measured in 2 results from 2 sources, far fewer than total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2014 reported inorganic arsenic at 8.3 µg/kg (mean) in rapeseed Oil, oil from European dietary-survey occurrence data.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>
